title: Anger test: do I have anger issues? Free anger self-check — cv.cm
description: Free anger test: rate 15 statements about how often you got angry over the past month, how strongly, how it came out and what it cost you, and get tips to manage anger. Not a diagnosis. Answers stay in your browser.
hint: Thinking about the past month, how well does each statement describe you?
scoreLabel: Anger self-check score (0 = few signs, 60 = many)
lede: Do small things set you off, or does anger linger for hours and spill onto the people you love? Rate 15 statements about the past month to see how much anger is affecting you, and what can help.
about: Anger is a normal, healthy emotion: it tells you something feels unfair or threatening and gives you energy to act. It becomes a problem when it comes too often or too strongly, lasts long after the moment, comes out as shouting, threats or breaking things, or damages your relationships, work or health. Problem anger is often tied to stress, poor sleep, pain, alcohol, anxiety or low mood, and it responds well to help: anger management skills and cognitive behavioral therapy work for most people.

The statements here were written for cv.cm around the main sides of problem anger: how often and how intensely it comes, how it's expressed, how long it lasts and what it costs. They are not the State-Trait Anger Expression Inventory or any other questionnaire, and they haven't been clinically validated, so the score bands are a rough guide, not clinical cut-offs. This check can't diagnose anything.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree), so the total runs from 0 to 60. 24 or less shows few signs of problem anger, 25 to 39 some and 40 or more many.

faq.q: How do I know if I have anger issues?
faq.a: Signs include getting angry often over small things, struggling to calm down, saying or doing things you regret, and people around you walking on eggshells. If anger is hurting your relationships or work, it's worth getting help.

faq.q: How can I calm down quickly?
faq.a: Notice the early signs, like a racing heart or clenched jaw, and step away before you react. Breathe slowly, count, go for a walk, and come back to the problem when you're calm.

faq.q: Where can I get help with anger?
faq.a: A doctor, counselor or psychologist can help, and many places run anger management courses. If you've hurt someone, or are afraid you might, get help now.

items: I got angry more often than most people around me.
Small things, like a slow driver or a late reply, set me off.
When I got angry, it came on fast and strong.
I raised my voice or shouted at someone.
I said things in anger that I later regretted.
I slammed, threw or hit things when I was angry.
My anger stayed with me for hours after the moment passed.
I kept going over things that had made me angry.
I felt my body tense up, my heart race or my face get hot with anger.
People around me seemed careful not to upset me.
Anger caused problems with my partner, family or friends.
Anger caused problems at work or school.
Once I was angry, I found it hard to calm down.
I felt irritable or on edge for much of the day.
I felt my anger was out of my control.

low.name: Few signs of problem anger (0–24)
low.body: Anger doesn't seem to be causing you much trouble right now. Everyone gets angry sometimes, and that's healthy when it's expressed calmly. Keep the habits that help you: noticing when you're getting wound up, taking a pause and saying what bothers you before it builds. Whatever your score, if anger has led you to hurt someone or break things, talk to a doctor or counselor.

moderate.name: Some signs of problem anger (25–39)
moderate.body: Anger seems to be getting the better of you some of the time. Try to notice your early warning signs, take a break before you respond, and look at what's feeding it: stress, poor sleep, alcohol or too much on your plate. If it keeps happening or starts to hurt your relationships, talk to a doctor or counselor. If it has led you to hurt someone or break things, don't wait: get help now.

high.name: Many signs of problem anger (40–60)
high.body: Your answers show anger that comes often or strongly and is costing you. That's hard to live with, and it's very treatable: anger management courses and therapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy help most people, so please talk to a doctor or counselor. If you've hurt someone, or worry that you might, get help now, and in an emergency call your local emergency number. Stress often sits behind anger; the stress check below can help you see how much.
